guides.title: More hobby words: building, paint and finish
guides.summary: Plain meanings for sprue, flash, dry fit, opaque, medium, retarder, tide mark, matte and satin, warm and cool, and tabletop standard.
body: Building words. Sprue: the plastic frame the parts come on. The small stubs left where a part joined it are often called nubs. Flash: thin, papery plastic or metal that leaked past the mould, trimmed off with a knife. Mould line: the faint raised ridge where the two halves of the mould met, scraped away before priming.

Dry fit: holding or taping parts together without glue to check how they line up, and to spot a nub or mould line stopping a joint sitting flush. Sub-assembly: a group of parts left unglued, such as a head, arms or a rider, so each can be painted on its own and glued on at the end.

Paint words. Opaque: covers what is under it. Translucent or see-through: lets the colour underneath show, as washes, glazes, inks and one-coat paints do. Coverage: how well a paint hides what is below in one coat. Pale and bright colours such as yellow and white often cover poorly and need several thin coats.

Medium: a clear liquid, binder with no pigment, mixed into paint. Glaze or thinning medium makes paint more see-through without breaking it up, and is the usual answer when a guide says to cut a wash with medium. One-coat medium is the same idea made for one-coat paints and does the same job in a wash. Flow improver is different: a strong additive used a drop at a time.

Retarder: a medium that slows drying, handy for wet blending or in a warm room. Tide mark: a hard dark ring left where a wash or glaze dried at the edge of a pool, also called a coffee ring. Lifting pools with a damp brush before they dry stops them forming.

Finish words. Matte: flat, no shine. Satin: a soft sheen. Gloss: shiny and smooth. They describe paint and varnish alike. Gloss helps washes run and transfers sit down, and a matte varnish at the end evens out mixed shine so the colours read properly.

Warm and cool. Warm colours are the reds, oranges and yellows; cool ones are the blues, blue-greens and violets. Warm tones seem to come forward and cool ones to sit back. It's relative: a purple leaning to red looks warm beside blue, and one leaning to blue looks cool beside orange. Every colour has warmer and cooler versions, such as an egg-yolk yellow and a lemon.

Tabletop standard: every area painted in its own colour, with a shade, a highlight and a finished base, so the model reads well at arm's length in a unit. Display level adds smooth blends and crisp fine detail for close viewing.

guides.title: Real skin tones: depth and undertone
guides.summary: Describe any real skin by how light or deep it's and which way it leans, then choose a base, shade and highlight to match.
body: Real skin covers a wide range, and no heritage, country or label gives you a fixed recipe. People with the same background can be very light or very deep. Describe the tone you want by two things instead: its depth, from very light to very deep, and its undertone, the colour it leans towards.

Undertones fall into a few families. Rosy or pink leans cool. Golden or peachy leans warm yellow. Olive has a muted yellow-green cast. Neutral sits between them. Deep skin can lean warm red-brown, umber or cool blue-violet. Nearly all living skin sits in the orange to brown family, so you're nudging an orange-brown, not inventing a new colour.

Set the depth first. A mid brown lifted with off-white covers most light and mid tones, and red and blue mixed to a deep brown makes a good base for very deep skin. Highlight size is a second control: the same paints read lighter with broad highlights and deeper with small, tight ones and more of the surface left dark.

Then steer the undertone with small amounts. A touch more red or pink for a rosy tone. Ochre or yellow for golden skin. For olive, a tiny drop of violet brown in the mid tone, or a thin flesh glaze over an ochre coat. A dot of blue in the darkest brown cools deep skin, and a red-leaning brown base warms it.

Very light skin: build from pinks and pale flesh with little brown, since brown reads as a tan. It can carry a lot of darker tone in the shadows and still read pale, as long as the raised areas stay clean and light. Cool the highlights slightly and keep the shadows warm.

Mid and golden skin: a warm amber or tan base, a soft warm brown wash, the base back on the raised areas, then a paler, slightly pearly tan on top. For a sun-darkened look, start a little lighter and glaze warmer browns down over it rather than mixing the base muddy.

Deep skin: base dark and leave most of it dark, lifting the brow, cheekbones, nose, lips and knuckles. Warm deep skin highlights towards a warm tan or bone; cool deep skin towards a blue-tinged grey, with only tiny dots of a pale shine. Glaze thin red into the lips, under the cheekbones and round the eyes so it looks alive.

Freckled fair skin: dot a thinned soft brown in a loose band across the nose and cheeks, and glaze a little warm red on the cheeks, nose and ears. Paint any red hair as muted orange and auburn rather than true red. To work from a photo of a real person, see Matching a real person's skin tone.

guides.title: Painting with colour blindness
guides.summary: Lean on light and dark rather than hue, label your paints, check colours with your phone and pick schemes that read by value.
body: Plenty of people see colour differently, most often finding reds, greens and browns hard to tell apart, and paint very well. What makes a model read on the table is mostly value, how light or dark each part is, and you can judge that without naming the colour.

Work by value. Plan each area as light, mid or dark, keep neighbouring parts at different values, and check with a black and white photo on your phone. If the model reads in greyscale, it will read in colour.

Label everything. Write the colour name big on the lid or side of each pot, keep paints in rows by colour family, and make a swatch card with the name beside each dab so you can see the dried colour and know what it is.
Mix and paint by recipe, not by eye. Save every step with the paint name, and write mixes as drop counts, such as two drops to one, so the same colour comes out every time and later units match.

Check colours with your phone when unsure. Many phones have colour filter settings in their accessibility options, and free colour picker apps name the colour under the camera. Point one at a pot, a mix on the palette or a finished area.

Choose schemes that stay readable: one main colour with neutrals, strong light against dark, and pairs that differ in value as well as hue. Red against green at the same value can merge, while a dark colour with a pale trim reads for almost everyone.
A monochrome scheme, one colour from dark to light, or plain black, white and greys, takes hue choices away almost entirely and still looks striking.
Ask someone to check a tricky choice now and then, such as a skin tone or a red beside a green, and treat it as a second opinion rather than a test you have to pass.

guides.title: A first weathering job on a vehicle
guides.summary: A simple first routine for a tank or vehicle: sponge chips, a brown wash for grime and streaks, then soot and dust, stopping early.
body: You need very little: a torn scrap of packing foam held in tweezers, a dark brown paint, a brown wash, a soft old drybrush, a dusty khaki or the colour of your bases, and a black for soot. Silver is optional. Finish the paint job and put any transfers on first, so they get worn and dirtied with the rest.

Chips first. Dab the foam in the dark brown, then dab most of it off on paper towel until it leaves only fine specks. Test on the underside. Press lightly, without dragging, on edges, corners, hatches and the lower hull, where crew and ground knock it. Build up over a few light passes rather than one heavy one.
Keep chips small and uneven, mostly on edges with only a few on flat panels. For bare metal, sponge a little silver inside some of the bigger brown chips, keeping some brown showing round it.

Grime next, with the brown wash. Dot it under bolts, hatches and vents and pull it straight down with a damp brush so it fades into streaks. Run it along the lower hull just above the tracks or wheels, then soften its top edge upwards with a clean damp brush.

Soot and dust last. Work the black off a soft brush on tissue until it leaves only a grey haze, and circle it round exhaust tips and gun muzzles. Then drybrush the khaki or base colour over tracks, wheels and lower panels, heaviest near the ground and fading out going up. Let a little catch the transfers.
Check it at arm's length after each stage. Weathering is easy to add and hard to take back, so stop while you still like it. If one spot gets too heavy, paint the base colour back over it once dry.

Once it's all dry, a coat of matte varnish protects the chips and evens out the shine of the wash. The same order works on infantry: chips on armour edges and weapons, grime in recesses, then dust on boots and hems.
When you want more, Order of weathering, Sponge chipping, Rust and grime streaks and Soot and scorch marks each take one of these steps further.

guides.title: How many layers a tabletop model needs
guides.summary: For troops, a base, one shade and one or two highlights is enough; save extra layers for faces, leaders and display pieces.
body: For rank and file models, the steps that do most of the work are a clean base coat, one shade and the main colour laid back over the raised areas. At that point a unit reads well on the table. A first edge highlight is the next best step, and most troops can stop there.

So a trooper's cloak needs about three tones: the base, a wash or shade in the folds, and one or two lighter layers on the raised folds. Layering can run to five or more steps, but that is for leaders and display work.

Give more steps to the parts near the head. A face might get three or four highlights, the chest and arms one or two, and boots and lower legs none beyond the shade. People look at the face first, so that is where extra steps show.

Short of time, highlight only one or two colours: the one that covers most of every model, then the most eye catching one, such as gold. The middle layers between the shade and the top highlight are the first thing to drop.

Glazing and wet blending stop at the same point: once the join between tones doesn't jump out at arm's length. For gaming models that is often after two or three passes. More is for close photos and display.
Judge a unit as a group, not one model under a lamp. A zoomed phone photo makes a small model look far rougher than it does in person, and in a unit of ten the small flaws vanish.
Do the same steps neatly on every model in the unit. Repetition makes a simple scheme look strong, and it's easier to add one more step to all ten later than to undo extra work on one.
Write down the steps you used on the first model, then decide which to drop for the rest. Leaders can take the full set, with a second, paler highlight on corners, knuckles and the brow.

guides.title: Oil paints for a first-timer
guides.summary: Start with a few earthy tubes and odourless spirit, use oils as a wash over fully dry acrylic, and know the common slips and fixes.
body: You need very few tubes. A dark brown and an orange brown cover most washes, grime and rust. A black adds soot and dark grime, and a white gives dust and mist. Very cheap sets are often weak and gritty, so a few decent single tubes go further.

Thin and clean with odourless mineral spirit or a low odour white spirit, never water. Pour a little into a small jar with a lid, keep a second clean jar for moving paint on the model, and work with a window open.

Put a small blob on the palette and mix spirit into it a little at a time. Some painters mix on glossy card or a tile; others use plain paper or baking parchment, which draws out excess oil so it dries flatter. Very thin mixes can split and look grainy.

A good first job is an oil wash over a finished acrylic model. Let the acrylic dry fully. Many painters seal it first with gloss or satin varnish, which helps the wash run and wipe off and protects the paint. Brush the wash on, leave it a few minutes, then wipe the raised areas with a sponge or a brush with the faintest trace of spirit.

Wash won't wipe off the highlights: it sat too long or went onto a matte, grippy surface. A cotton bud or brush barely damp with spirit lifts it; next time wipe sooner, or varnish first. Never scrub, which can rub through to the paint.

Highlights stained darker: the longer the wash sits, the more it tints what is under it. Once the oil is dry and sealed with matte varnish, repaint the top highlights in acrylic. Acrylic lifting: that comes from scrubbing, or thin paint on unprimed plastic, so prime, seal, use a softer brush and press lightly.

Still tacky after days: oils dry slowly, often several days, and longer when thick or in greens and blues. Wait until a hidden spot no longer feels sticky before varnishing, as varnish over tacky oil can wrinkle or cloud. Keep a second model on the go while one dries.
Keep spirit away from the sticky tack on painting handles, which turns to goo. Don't paint acrylic straight onto wet or unsealed oil, as it can flake later; seal it with matte varnish first.

guides.title: A first NMM exercise: a straight sword
guides.summary: Practise painted metal on one blade: mark the light, step from dark grey to white in a few big jumps, then add bounce light and edges.
body: A straight blade is the best first try: two flat faces, an edge and a simple light pattern. Prime it black or dark grey and put out black, white and a mid grey, with a touch of blue to keep the greys cool. Mix a short ladder of four or five greys first, so you never stop halfway to mix.

Decide where the light comes from, usually above and a little in front, and the angle the model will mostly be seen from. With thin white, roughly mark the brightest band on the face tilted towards the light, ending each stroke where it should be lightest. It's only a guide.

Cover the blade in the mid grey in two thin coats. Then work up: add white to the grey and paint the light band again on a smaller area, then lighter and smaller again. Use about three steps, each a clear jump. A short, sudden change looks shinier than a long smooth blend.

Now the dark. Thin a darker grey and pull it towards the light from the other end, so the face runs from near black to near white. Put the darkest dark right against the brightest light somewhere; that hard meeting reads as polished. Keep little of the blade in plain mid grey, or it looks like stone.

Treat the two faces differently. The one tilted to the light gets the bright band; the one tilted down stays darker and can pick up a dull hint of the ground colour, such as a muted green or brown. A sharp line where the faces meet sells the edge.

Bounce light is a second, weaker shine on the side away from the main light, as if light bounced back off the ground or a wall. Add a small, dimmer band opposite the main highlight, kept apart from it by dark. Leaving it out is the usual reason a first try looks flat.

Finish with a thin pale grey line along the cutting edge, brightest where it crosses the main band, and one or two tiny near white dots at the brightest point. A filter, meaning a very thin, see-through tint over the whole blade such as a thin blue, can tie the steps together; keep it off the white dots.
It looks wrong until the edge and dots go on, so finish before judging, then check it in a black and white phone photo. Non-metallic steel and the Painted steel recipe take the same ideas further.

guides.title: One-coat paints through an airbrush
guides.summary: One-coat paints spray well once thinned with airbrush thinner, building colour in light passes over a pre-shaded undercoat.
body: One-coat paints go through an airbrush, like washes and inks do. They're thick in the pot, so thin them first: about two or three drops of airbrush thinner to one of paint is a common start, and any airbrush thinner works. A mid sized needle copes with most paints; a very fine one needs more careful thinning.

They suit spraying over a pre-shade or zenithal undercoat, such as black primer with white or light grey sprayed from above. The paint is see-through, so the undercoat shows through as shadow, midtone and highlight.

Spray light passes and let each dry before the next. The first coat often looks blotchy and evens out with more thin coats. Piling it on wet flattens the colour, as if you had never pre-shaded, and can spider or run.
More coats give a deeper colour with less contrast; fewer keep it brighter. The paint dries darker and more solid than it looks wet, so dry it with plain air and wait a minute before judging.

Spray a darker one-coat paint of the same colour into the shadows from below, so the shadows read as coloured rather than dull grey. Thinned much further with water and thinner, the same paints make a filter: a few light passes over the whole model that stain rather than cover and pull rough layers together.
Then brush the details as usual: small parts in solid colours, edge highlights, lenses and gems. For an army this is a cleaner, faster version of drybrush and tint.

Clean the airbrush straight after and between colours, as with any paint, using Cleaning an airbrush between colours. Seal the finished model with matte varnish, as these paints can rub off raised edges.

guides.title: Salt weathering
guides.summary: Stick coarse salt over a rust or metal base, spray the top colour, then rinse the salt off to leave patches of worn paint.
body: Salt works as a mask. Wherever a grain sits, the top colour can't reach, so rinsing it off later leaves patches of the colour underneath. It gives bigger, more random wear than sponge chipping, which suits rusty vehicles, scenery and old metal.
Prime, then paint the colour you want to show through, such as a rust brown, a dark brown or a dull metal. Varying the browns a little looks more natural. Let it dry fully.

Brush or spray a little hairspray onto the areas that should wear, such as edges, lower panels and places where water gathers. Sprinkle coarse salt onto it while it's wet. Crush or rub the salt first for smaller, finer chips, and use less of it for a subtle result.

Once the salt is stuck and dry, spray the top colour over everything in thin coats. An airbrush works best; a brush tends to shift the salt or leave weaker paint around it. Bright or pale top colours show the effect better than black.

When the top coat is dry, rinse the model under warm water and rub the salt away with your fingers, an old brush, or a toothpick for small spots. Cold water works poorly, and very hot water can warp plastic. The base colour shows wherever the salt was.

Paint that is too thick around a grain can tear off with it, so keep the top coat thin. Once dry, tidy the edges of the worn patches with a brush, and repaint any spot that looks wrong with more rust or the top colour.

Put the wear where it would really happen: edges that get handled and low areas where water and dirt collect. Too much salt looks messy rather than worn, so start small and test on a spare part first.
Salt also goes onto wet hairspray in Hairspray and scratch-through chipping, giving large patches as well as fine chips from the same top coat.

guides.title: Using masking fluid by brush
guides.summary: Brush liquid mask over parts or chip spots with an old soaped brush, let it dry, paint over it, then peel or rub it off.
body: Liquid mask is a rubbery liquid that dries to a film you peel off later. It isn't only for airbrush users: brush it over a finished part, such as a helmet or a gem, before painting next to it, or dab it where chips should be before a top coat.

It ruins brushes, so use an old cheap one, a sponge, or a cocktail stick for small dots. Rub a little liquid hand soap into the bristles before dipping, and wash the brush in soapy water straight after. Dried mask won't wash out with thinner.

Test it on a hidden spot first, and only over paint that has dried and gripped well. It can pull up fresh or poorly gripping paint, especially on soft or oily plastic. A light coat of gloss varnish under it helps it lift cleanly.

Lay it on with some body rather than a thin skim, as thin mask tears when you peel it. Two thin coats are steadier than one thick blob. Let it dry fully, roughly 15 to 30 minutes depending on the product and how thick it is; check the label.

Paint over and around it in thin coats, since thick paint bridges the edge and tears when the mask comes off. Once the paint is dry, peel the mask with tweezers or roll it onto a cocktail stick. Small bits rub off with a fingertip or a soft eraser.

For chips, dab mask with the hard side of a sponge or an old brush where wear would happen, over a rust or metal colour. Paint the top colour, then pull the mask off roughly: the paint comes away in ragged chips.
Peel it soon after the paint dries rather than days later, as old mask gets harder to remove. If you want a transfer or stencil chipped as well, put the mask under it, not on top.

guides.title: Matching a real person's skin tone
guides.summary: Paint a historical figure or portrait from a clear photo, reading depth, undertone and light rather than following a label.
body: For a historical figure, a portrait or a character with a particular look, work from a clear photo of a real person with that tone. One stock recipe for a whole group of people flattens them into a single colour, and real faces vary far more than any label suggests.
Judge the photo with its light in mind. The same face looks paler under office light and warmer and darker at sunset. Pick the light your model will sit in, and choose a photo lit in a similar way.

Read the real colours. A colour picker on a phone or computer shows tones that are usually duller and browner than you expect. Take three: the lit forehead or cheekbone, the main tone of the cheek, and the shadow under the jaw. Mix to those, then judge the dry paint beside the photo.

Turn the photo black and white, or squint, to see where the light and dark fall. Get the values right first and the colour second. A face with light and dark in the right places reads as real even if the hue is a little off.

Test each mix on a spare head, a bit of sprue or the base rim before the face. Swap steps between recipes you already know, such as one recipe's highlight over another's base, to get a new tone from the same paints.

One person's skin isn't one colour. Cheeks, nose, ears and knuckles run redder, the forehead a touch more yellow, and shadows and older skin cooler and bluer. Add these with thin glazes once the main tone is right.

If the tone drifts: too orange, mix in a little light cool blue. Too yellow, a thin flesh or pink glaze pulls it back. Grey and lifeless, a very thin warm orange flesh glaze over the whole area brings it back to life.

For a group of real people, such as a crew or a regiment, vary depth and undertone from figure to figure as a real group would, and keep one shared shade colour or final highlight so they still read as one unit.

guides.title: Painting holograms and projected figures
guides.summary: Paint a hologram as a see-through glow: thin bright glazes over white, a lit emitter and a little light spilling nearby.
body: A hologram reads as light, not a solid thing: pale, glowing and slightly see-through, in one colour, often a cool blue or green. Paint it with glow methods rather than normal shading, and ignore the real colours of skin, cloth and kit inside it, so the whole figure looks projected.

Base the projected figure white. Mix a translucent bright colour about half and half with glaze medium, since neat paint darkens instead of glowing, and glaze it all over with a big-bellied brush. Add further glazes starting lower down so the colour deepens towards the bottom and in the recesses.
Keep the palest tone on the top-most points, with a few thin white highlights. Pick out eyes, folds and buckles in a pale tint of the same colour rather than their real colours.

For a flickering, broken signal, paint the final pale lines as broken pieces, stopping and restarting them along the form, as you would on painted lightning. Judge it from normal viewing distance; close up it always looks rougher than it is.
Paint the emitter as a glowing source: white first, then glazes of the hologram colour, deepest away from its brightest point, which stays near white. A thin near black line round it makes it pop.

Spill a little of the colour onto nearby surfaces that face the hologram or the emitter: thin glazes of a mid tone, then a very light drybrush moving outwards. Only surfaces that can see the light catch it, and nothing should be as bright as the source.

If the hologram is a clear plastic part, a coat of satin varnish works as a primer without clouding it. Tint it with inks and thin glazes so light still passes through, and fix it with a tiny dot of glue.

guides.title: Rain, water drops and wet surfaces
guides.summary: Show wet armour, skin and cloth with darker colour and chosen gloss, rain streaks that run straight down and raised drops.
body: Water makes a surface darker and shinier, and a matte surface beside it makes the shine read more. Before committing, brush plain water over the area: while it's wet you see roughly how gloss will look.

Wet armour and metal: brush slightly thinned gloss varnish over the plates, keeping it out of the recesses. It deepens the colour underneath, and brushed gloss comes out shinier than sprayed. Keep cloth, hair and skin around it matte so the contrast stays strong.
Wet or sweaty skin: a wash that dries glossy, or a very thin touch of satin over the finished skin, leaves a sheen. Keep it light and to a few areas, as full gloss makes skin and cloth look odd.

Rain streaks: rain runs straight down vertical faces. Pull thin, slightly darker lines down from edges, rivets and seams. Old stains look hazy and matte; a few thin, dark, glossy lines look like water running right now.

Raised drops: a dab of thick gloss on an edge or a hanging strand forms a drop. For a bigger one, glue a short brush bristle as a core and build gloss or clear effect onto its end in coats, letting each dry so it gathers into a teardrop.

Painted drops on a flat surface: paint each drop a little darker than the surface under it, add a tiny white glint on the side facing the light, then a dot of gloss on top. Vary the size, and keep them on upper surfaces and hanging from lower edges.

Puddles on the base: small pools of clear gloss gel or resin at low points read as fresh rain, especially next to dead matte rust or mud. Do every gloss step last, after any matte varnish, and blow dust off first, because gloss fixes it in place.

guides.title: Frost and icicles on armour and models
guides.summary: Cool the highlights, dust frost onto top edges, paint glassy ice over a strong blue and hang icicles where meltwater would drip.
body: Frost starts with the light. Highlight the whole model with a cool grey or pale blue rather than a warm cream, so it reads as cold before any ice goes on. Grey gloves and blue-grey tones elsewhere help.

For a light frosty crust on armour, brush a fine powdery snow mix thinly along the top edges and upper surfaces, or dab off-white on with a nearly dry scrap of sponge. With an airbrush, a light whitish veil over the painted area reads as thin frost. Commit to it: a timid dusting tends to look like a mistake.

Thick, glassy ice on a part: base a strong, saturated blue, then dab and criss-cross many very thin coats of white to suggest facets, leaving some blue showing. Glaze a thinned pale icy blue over it, and dab white along the edges as chips rather than a smooth line.

Icicles: draw thin strings of hot glue onto baking parchment, not wax paper, and peel them off once cool. Or warm thin clear plastic above a candle, never in the flame, and pull it into points. Glue them flat side to the model with tweezers.
Icicles glued onto paint hold weakly, because the bond is only to the paint. Fix them to bare plastic before painting where you can, or brush two coats of gloss varnish over them for extra hold.

Hang icicles where meltwater would run down and freeze, not at random: under the lower edges of plates, a cloak hem, a barrel or a ledge. A few tiny icicles suggest a light frost; many suggest deep cold.
Paint icicles with a little white in clear medium for frosted, half see-through ice; clear on its own reads as liquid water. Add thin pale blue where they're thickest and white on their edges.

Keep frost and snow matte and powdery, and ice and icicles glossy; the difference in finish sells both. For cold skin, shade with blue, highlight with a cold off-white and glaze a little red onto the cheeks, nose and ears.

guides.title: Painting banners and flags
guides.summary: Paint banners off the model on a flat base colour, shade each colour with its own darker tone, then add the design and wear.
body: Paint the banner or flag before it goes on the model where you can, as freehand takes a lot of handling. If it has to be on, wear a glove or wrap the rest in cling film. Lay the design on a flat base colour first and shade the background after, since repairs are far easier on flat paint.

A big flag is the largest flat area on the model, so it pulls the eye. If it would be bright red, start from a muted, drabber version and keep the purest colour for the focal point. Flags mostly use three colours, which is a good limit.

Shade each colour with a darker related tone: brown under red, beige under white, dark blue under blue. One shade over every colour looks wrong; a yellow flag shaded dark red looks dirty. Keep the shade in the troughs of the folds and pull thinned highlights onto the ridges and the outer edge.

Washes run down a hanging banner and pool at the bottom edge. Thin them with medium, use small amounts, and lay the banner flat to dry, one side at a time. Lift any pooling with a clean damp brush while it's wet.

Sketch the design on paper first, then mark it lightly in pencil on the dry base colour. Find the centre from the top edge, not a ragged bottom, and paint one line straight down following the cloth. Build the emblem from simple lines through that centre, then thicken them. A white or yellow emblem on a red, blue or black field, or the reverse, reads from across the table.

Small emblems can be highlighted on their own, ignoring the folds, so they stand out. For transfers, gloss the cloth first so they slide into place, then chip their edges with the cloth colours and drag thin stains over them so they sit in the fabric.

For an old, hard-used banner, wet blend a few drab tones with downward strokes so it looks streaked by rain, darken the bottom edge and nick the edges with small notches as if torn. For a white flag, ivory over a warm grey covers far better than pure white.

guides.title: Digital pixel camouflage
guides.summary: Build digital camo from small stepped squares in three or four tones of one colour family, by tape and spray or by brush.
body: Digital camo is made of small squares and stepped, staircase edges instead of blobs. Pick three or four tones from one colour family that suit the setting, each clearly darker than the last, or two of them will read as one.

With tape and spray: cut narrow tape into strips. For each patch, lay two strips at a right angle and a third cut into a stepped edge below them, and press them down hard over raised detail so they seal. Spray, mask the next set, spray again, then peel gently.

By brush: paint each patch as a cluster of small squares, outlining the edges first with the tip and keeping the corners square. Let patches of each tone touch the others rather than float alone, and vary their size so nothing repeats.

At small scale or on busy, curved parts, use fewer tones and bigger, simpler steps, as with any camo. On troops, keep the pattern to one area, such as the trousers or a cloak, so it doesn't hide the figure's shape.

Shade and highlight the base colour first so the pattern sits in light and shadow, then highlight all the camo as one area. Satin varnish before washes and weathering, and a thin all-over wash, tie the pattern together.

guides.title: Painting insect wings
guides.summary: Paint fly, wasp and dragonfly wings as shimmering panels: white where the light hits, a purple wash, and rings of dabbed colour.
body: Insect wings are thin and glassy, so treat them as tinted panels catching light rather than solid skin. Paint them off the model where you can; they're fragile and easy to smudge.

For an iridescent fly wing, paint white on the top of the wing where the light hits and leave the lower part darker, as light passes through there. Pick out the edges and veins in white too, then give the whole wing a purple wash, moving it about so it doesn't pool where you don't want it.

Set the sheen colours out on the palette in order. Dab a bright green into the middle of the wing, then a mix of green and yellow round it, then yellow and pink, then pink at the outer edge. Dabbing copies the spotty look of a real wing; thin glazes in soft patches work too. A touch of white helps a colour cover over the dark parts.

Finish with thin white along the top edge, the torn edges and where the cells meet, keeping it off the veins, then a second dabbed layer for texture and a few dots of bright white at the very top. Slim any veins you lost with the purple, and dab tiny bits of the sheen colours back round the white so it doesn't look chalky.

For a colour-shift look, base a rich mid colour such as purple. Drybrush one hue from above, such as pinks, and another from below, such as deep blue then turquoise, and finish both sides with the same pale yellow.
Veins: run a thin dark line along each sculpted vein on a pale wing, or a pale one on a dark wing, and keep them finer than you think. Edge torn ends with a light colour so the tear reads.

Clear plastic wings: a coat of satin varnish works as a primer without clouding them. Tint them with inks and thin glazes so light still passes through, add the veins, and fix them with a tiny dot of glue.

Hard, shiny beetle wing cases: a near black purple base, a muted purple on the curves, a thin pale violet line on top of each and a small teal glaze on each plate for an oily sheen, then a touch of gloss.

guides.title: Velvet and fur trim
guides.summary: Stipple velvet into a soft, deep, matte cloth, and paint fur trim and ermine with tinted greys, flicked strands and spots.
body: Velvet is soft and matte, so keep its highlights broad and gentle and its shadows deep and rich. That sets it apart from shiny silk, where highlights are small and sharp. A deep plum red (#5a1020) stippled up to a soft pinkish red (#c85a5a) is a classic velvet.

Build velvet by stippling: dab tiny dots of each mix along the blend, from the top highlight down, leaving a little space between dots. The dots hide the joins between layers and give the slightly fuzzy texture that reads as velvet.

Then glaze thin base colour over the edges of the stippled areas, reaching further in with each thinner glaze and sweeping towards the shadow. A slightly see-through warm highlight, such as a pale warm flesh over purple, avoids the chalky look white gives.

Fur trim on a cloak or collar: base it, wash it, then flick lighter strokes along the direction of the fur in stages, each finer than the last. Paint the cloth up to it neatly and keep the line where fur meets cloth clear.

White fur trim: plain greys look flat. Use greys tinted with purple, brown or blue for the shadows and a dusky pink or warm off-white for the top highlights, keeping the brightest white to a few strands near the face.

Ermine, the white fur with small black tail tips seen on the robes of kings and nobles: finish the white fur first, then paint the dark tips with a thinned dark one-coat paint so it sinks into the texture. One light drybrush over the whole trim makes spots and fur read as one material.

guides.title: Rubber tyres, hoses and cables
guides.summary: Paint rubber, tyres and cables a soft near black so they separate from black armour, then dust or dirty the treads.
body: Rubber is a soft black. Base tyres, hoses, cables and flexible joints in a very dark grey rather than pure black, and keep true black for hard armour and for shading. The two then read as different materials.

Line the ridges of cables and the tread of tyres with true black, then edge highlight in a dark grey, with a lighter grey only on the sharpest corners. On a black model, one subtle grey step along the edges is often enough, so the rubber stays darker than the armour.

On ribbed cables and tyre tread, wipe almost all the paint off the brush and skim along so only the raised ribs catch it. A smooth round hose has no edge to follow: skim one line down the side facing the light.

Highlight black pipes and hoses with a fairly light grey, not just a dark one, or they vanish into the model. Coloured hoses work too: an orange base under a yellow one-coat paint, with a thin pale yellow highlight, makes small tubes pop.
Hazard-striped cables: paint and shade the cable yellow, plot thin slanted black stripes faintly so they spiral round it, thicken them until both bands match, and tidy any wobbles with the yellow.
Leave push-fit wheels and tyres off the model, paint them on their own and fit them at the end. It saves brushing black round every edge.

Dusty tyres: brush a light earth enamel or oil, thinned a little, into the tread, wait about 20 to 30 minutes, then wipe it off the raised parts with a brush damp with thinner. Or work dry earth pigment into the tread and lower rim. A well thinned wash of the base ground colour ties the wheels to the base.

guides.title: Books, bottles, candles and small props
guides.summary: Small props read best with clean edges and one clear material each: crisp page edges, glassy bottles, soft waxy candles.
body: Props are small, so separate each one from its neighbour with a fine dark line and give it one clear material. Paint the hard to reach areas first, then the props in front of them, such as books and bottles held in hands.

Books: base the cover in a leather or cloth colour and highlight only a short line along its edges and corners. Define the page edges by hand in a pale bone or parchment tone with fine dark lines between them, as a wash may not pick them out. Writing on open pages is tiny dark brown squiggles in rows.

Bottles, jars and potions: paint them as glass, following Painting glass and clear parts. A dark edge, a gradient across, a sharp white glint near the opposite corner, liquid kept level with the ground, and gloss on the glass only.

Candles: wax looks soft, so blend gently with no hard steps. Base a pale greyish green (#c9c9a0) or bone dulled with light brown, work up through pale cream (#e3dcc0) and take the top edge and drip tips near white (#f6f4ec). Darken the base mix for older candles.
Extra drips on candles: dab white glue, thinned only slightly so it holds its shape, down the sides with a toothpick, let it dry, then add more on the same spots so each drip grows fatter and longer.
Wax seals on letters and scrolls want a colour unlike the main accent, such as a deep burgundy (#4a1420), highlighted by mixing in a little pale blue-grey and finished with a touch of gloss.

guides.title: Ships, sails and rigging
guides.summary: Paint hull, deck and sails as separate parts, treat sails as canvas and give rigging and tarred rope a darker rope tone.
body: Keep masts and sails off the hull while you paint where the kit allows, and base each part in its own colour. Painting all the hulls first, then all the sails in one session, keeps a fleet consistent.

Hull and deck are wood: follow the planks along their length, as in Painting wood grain. A plank-coloured deck looks more natural than a black one. Pull any grime and streaks straight down the hull sides, the way water runs.

Sails are canvas. Block in a dark ivory or pale tan, run a thinned khaki into the creases and dark brown only into the deepest folds, restore the flat areas, then highlight the outer edges and the crests of the billows. Keep the shade in the troughs and lead the highlights onto the ridges.

Old sails: wet blend a few drab tones with downward strokes so they look stained, and nick the edges for tears. Designs on sails can be freehand or picked out from cast detail; paint them on the flat colour before shading. One accent colour on sails and flags ties a ship together.

Rope and rigging: base a light sandy beige, wash brown so it runs into the twists, then highlight back along each twist with a finer pale cream on top. For tarred rope, base it a very dark brown, wash it black and keep the highlight to a dull brown on the top of each twist.

guides.title: Snake and serpent patterns
guides.summary: Lay out a snake's bands, stripes or diamonds before highlighting, then light each colour in its own tones over a pale belly.
body: Snakes and serpents are mostly pattern. Block in the whole pattern first, base colour and markings, before any highlights. Mistakes are easy to fix at that stage, and the highlights stay consistent along the body.
Then highlight each colour in its own tones: blues and teals on a blue base, greys on black markings. Keep the gaps between scales dark so each scale stands out, and edge only the most raised ones.

Bands and stripes: mark them faintly first, evenly spaced along the body and slanting slightly so they wrap round it, then thicken them and tidy wobbles with the base colour. Diamonds: place a small dot at each point along the spine, join the dots, then fill the shapes in thin coats.

Body colours often shift from a dark back through the flanks to a paler belly. A deep slate blue back (#1f3b57), blue-green flanks (#3f7f7a), then grey-green to magenta and a pale lilac (#c6a9d8) on the belly scales makes a vivid serpent.
For a pale belly, base a mid blue (#4a6a9a), shade a muted violet-grey (#4a4058) between the scales, then lighten it step by step with off-white. It reads as a pale underside without going chalky.
Eyes: a soft white, a pale colour glazed lighter in the middle, a darker rim of wash, and a thin vertical black slit for the pupil. A thin line reads more reptilian than a dot. Gloss the eyes last.

guides.title: Painting robots and mechs
guides.summary: Treat robot and mech armour as flat lit panels, paint the inner frame first, then add panel lines, stripes and grease.
body: Robots and mechs sit between vehicles and armoured figures. Their armour is flat planes and corners, so give each face its own light level: faces towards the light clearly lighter, faces turned away clearly darker. See Highlighting blocky, angular shapes.

Leave arms and big plates off so you can reach the frame and joints. Paint the inner machinery first, while nothing around it's finished: silver, a black wash, a few bronze bolts, a dark brown wash for an oily look, then a bright silver drybrush.

Snap-fit poseable kits: pull them apart and plug every socket and peg with small bits of tape or putty, and leave hidden inner frame parts bare. Paint in the joints makes poses sag or parts stop fitting.

Prime for the armour colour even if there is a lot of metal, as painting white over silver is much harder than the other way round. If a wash leaves big panels murky, drybrush the base colour back over the blotches, then layer thinned base into the panel centres.

Panel lines: gloss varnish the armour, dot a thinned dark enamel wash into the lines so it runs along them, and wipe stray wash off flat panels with a cotton bud damp with thinner. Work with good airflow, add any transfers, then matte varnish.

Hazard stripes go where moving parts are dangerous: joints, pistons and weapons. Paint a pale band, then diagonal stripes at about 45 degrees from the middle outwards, one stripe width apart. Tidy overspill with the armour colour, and use rivets and panel lines as guides.

Pistons and joints: bright silver stroked round the piston, a gritty texture paint in ball joints for caked grime, then a glossy oil-coloured enamel or oil pulled out from the joint. A few glossy grease spots on a satin or matte robot look good.
Small drones and gadgets: prime dark silver, wash black, drop bright orange into the lower recesses as rust, drybrush steel, then pick out lenses in red and cables in bright colours.

guides.title: Board game and soft plastic figures
guides.summary: Bendy board game figures need a good wash, a sliced not scraped mould line, a primer that grips and varnish at the end.
body: Most board game figures are made from a softer, bendier plastic than hobby kits, often PVC. It's tough and cheap to make in big numbers, and the detail can be good, but it flexes, often carries an oily release agent from the mould, and plastic glue doesn't weld it.

Wash the figures first in warm soapy water with an old toothbrush, rinse and let them dry fully. Release agent left on the surface stops primer and paint gripping, and paint that beads up or rubs off is the usual sign.

Mould lines are the hard part. Scraping and filing, which work on hard plastic, just raise burrs on soft plastic. Instead, lay a fresh blade almost flat and slice the line off in small, slow cuts, and change the blade as soon as it skips rather than cuts. On a quick game piece, take off only the lines that show.

Bent spears and swords can be warmed, straightened and cooled to set the shape; factories do the same with fresh parts. Dip the part in hot water until it softens, hold it straight and cool it under cold water. Results vary: some soft plastics hardly respond to heat, so try a hidden part first.

Use super glue for any building. On the softest, waxy plastics even super glue grips poorly, so a joint that keeps failing is better pinned: drill a tiny hole in each part and glue in a short piece of fine wire.

Always prime. Thin hobby paint beads on bare soft plastic and rubs off easily. A spray primer grips well; a brush-on surface primer in two or three very thin coats lasts better than one thick coat. Some painters brush on a primer made for soft plastic first.

Paint them as any figure, often with a quick routine such as Base, wash and tidy method. Because the plastic flexes, paint can crack or chip on bendy parts, so finish anything that gets handled with a couple of thin varnish coats, and expect the odd touch up on spears and swords.
Figures that came pre-painted can be painted over once washed; see Repainting toys and pre-painted figures.

guides.title: Plastic, resin, metal and prints compared
guides.summary: Each model material needs its own glue, clean up and primer care, so knowing which one you have saves early mistakes.
body: Hard plastic kits on frames are the most common. They're light and tough, clean up easily with a knife and sanding stick, and plastic glue welds them together. Fresh paint on bare plastic rubs off easily, which is one good reason to prime.

Soft plastic, used for most board game figures, bends rather than snaps. Mould lines are hard to remove, plastic glue does nothing to it and paint needs a primer to grip. Board game and soft plastic figures covers it.

Cast resin holds very sharp detail but is brittle and can shatter if dropped. Wash off the mould release first, cut casting blocks away in small bites, file gently and glue with super glue; plastic glue does nothing to it. Wear a mask when cutting or sanding resin, as the dust is harmful.

Metal, often called white metal or pewter, is heavy, so arms and weapons need pins as well as super glue. It's harder to file, dulls blades quickly and cracks if bent back and forth. Paint chips off it more easily than off plastic, so varnish it. Very old metal figures may contain lead, so wear gloves when stripping or filing them.

Resin 3D prints hold fine detail like cast resin and glue the same way, but they must be washed and fully cured, and thin parts are often brittle. Filament prints are tough and cheap but show layer lines, so they suit terrain more than figures.

Some smaller makers now use other injection moulded plastics. The softer kinds behave like board game plastic; the harder kinds file and scrape almost like a normal kit. Neither takes plastic glue, so use super glue.

Not sure what you have? Metal is much heavier than it looks. Hard plastic usually comes on frames. Soft plastic bends easily in your fingers. Resin parts often come on chunky casting blocks and can feel waxy or oily before washing.
Glue rule of thumb: plastic glue only for hard plastic to hard plastic; super glue for every other material and for mixed joins; two-part epoxy or a pin for heavy joints.
keywords: is my model resin or plastic

guides.title: Hand tools for building models
guides.summary: A knife, clippers, files, sanding sticks, a cutting mat, tweezers and a pin vice cover nearly all building work.
body: A hobby knife or scalpel with spare blades does most clean up. Cut away from your body and fingers in several small strokes rather than one hard push. Hold it near the tip for fine work and further up the handle for power. A blunt blade needs more force, and that is when it slips, so change blades often; bulk packs of scalpel blades cost far less.

Keep a curved blade for hollows and between hair strands. For scraping mould lines a slightly worn blade is better than a brand new one, which can skip and leave ridges, so move a blade from cutting to scraping once it starts to dull.
A self-healing cutting mat protects the table, closes up after cuts and gives a firm surface to brace a part on while you trim it. Pick one in a colour that dropped parts stand out on.

Needle files take material off fast and suit metal and resin, but leave scratches on plastic. Sanding sticks and sponges do most plastic work: around 320 to 400 grit for nubs and heavy lines, 600 to 800 for tight spots, then 1200 or finer for smooth surfaces. Sanding sponge bends round curves.
Wet the paper or file so it clogs less and keeps the dust down, and wear a mask when sanding resin, metal or putty. Sand in one direction only to keep a sharp edge or point.

Fine pointed tweezers place tiny parts, transfers and tufts. Reverse grip tweezers stay closed until you squeeze them, so they hold a part or a scrap of sponge without hand ache. Cheap pairs work as well as hobby branded ones.

A pin vice, a small hand drill, makes holes for pins and gun barrels. Turn it one way only, with light pressure; turning it back can loosen the bit. The bits that come with cheap drills are often poor, so a set of fine bits is worth adding.
Flat faced clippers free parts from the frame. Keep a fine pair for delicate plastic and an old pair for thick frames, wire and paper clips, which notch good blades.

guides.title: Checking a second-hand lot
guides.summary: Look a used lot over for paint, glue, damage and missing parts, then sort it into models to fix, strip or keep as spares.
body: Ask for clear, close photos before agreeing a price. Blurry pictures hide half-empty frames, loose bits in bags and a mix of models that may not make up what you want.

Look at the paint. Thin, sound paint can be painted over or touched up; thick coats that blur the detail mean stripping. Resin is the hardest material to strip cleanly, so a thickly painted resin model is more work. A big model in many parts can take longer to strip than to repair and prime.

Look at the joins. Superglued parts can usually be popped apart and reglued, while plastic glue joints have to be cut. Loose or crooked parts, glue blobs and gaps are all fixable but take time. Many second-hand models were built without the mould lines removed, so plan to clean those too.

Check the thin parts: spears, antennae, horns and swords. Old metal figures often have bent weapons, which can be eased back with gentle warmth, but metal snaps if bent back and forth. Snapped parts can be pinned or replaced with wire.
Check every part is there, against a photo of the complete model if you can. Paint and damage matter little if the parts you want are whole, and a box of odd parts is still useful for conversions.
Very old metal figures may contain lead. Wear gloves when stripping or filing them, keep the dust down and wash your hands afterwards.
Before stripping someone's paint job, take a photo of it, as an old scheme can still give you ideas. Then sort the lot into models to touch up, models to strip and parts for the spares box.
keywords: what to look for in used models

guides.title: Brush-on varnish without smearing
guides.summary: Brush varnish on in thin coats without going back over it, and seal one-coat paints and inks first so the brush can't drag their colour.
body: Brush or spray? Spray is the quickest way to coat a whole model and gives the smoothest finish, but it's fussy about cold and damp air. Brush-on is slower, works in any weather and lets you pick a finish for each part. Many painters spray whole models and keep a brush-on pot for bases, touch-ups and small repairs.

The catch with a brush is that water-based varnish is wet, and some paints soften again when wet. One-coat contrast-style paints, inks and some washes can lift and smear under the brush, and reds and golds can creep into a white next to them. The thin, staining paints are the ones to watch.

So give those paints longer before you varnish, at least an hour and more if you can, as touch dry isn't fully dry. Then treat the first coat as a seal: a light mist of spray if you have it, or one thin brushed coat laid down in a single pass with no scrubbing. Once that is dry, later coats can't reach the paint.

Shake the pot well and pour a little into a palette well rather than working from the pot. Use a soft synthetic brush, a wide flat one for big areas. Lay the varnish on like a thin all-over wash and move any pools out of recesses before they set. Work with flat surfaces facing up where you can, and go thinner on upright faces so it doesn't run.

Never go back over a patch that has started to dry. Varnish forms a skin as it dries, and brushing it again tears the skin and leaves streaks, bumps and lifted colour. If you missed a spot, wait until it's dry and catch it on the next coat.

Keep coats thin and let each dry fully. One or two thin coats is plenty, as a thick coat can dry cloudy or milky and fill fine detail. Some painters add a drop of water to help it flow; others use matte straight from the pot, as water can make it less flat. Thinning a gloss tones its shine down.

Brushed varnish often comes out a little shinier than sprayed, and brush-on matte is usually a touch less flat than matte spray. If it dries with a sheen, another thin coat of a flatter matte sorts it. Leave the model 12 to 24 hours before heavy handling, or check the label.
If it has already smeared, let it dry fully first. Paint the original colour back over the stain, or tidy a stained white with white, then seal that area with a light first coat before you carry on.

guides.title: Photographing models with just a phone
guides.summary: One lamp, a sheet of paper and a steady phone take good model photos, with no lightbox or proper camera needed.
body: Light matters far more than the camera. A phone takes good photos of a model under good, steady light, and an expensive camera won't save a badly lit one.

Tape a sheet of plain paper or card to a wall or a box and let it curve down onto the desk under the model, so there is no line behind it. White, grey or black all work, and a dark backdrop makes the model look brighter. Stand the model a little in front of the curve so its shadow doesn't fall on the paper.

With one lamp, put it right beside the phone, or above and just behind it, pointing at the front of the model. Light from straight above casts real shadows over the ones you painted and burns out the top. Your painting lamp is fine if it's a daylight colour. Prop a white card or sheet of paper on the far side to bounce light into the shadows.

If the lamp gives hard shadows or glare, tape baking parchment or tracing paper over it, or move it back a little. Switch the other lights off, close the blinds and turn the flash off: mixed light gives odd colours and flash flattens your shading.

You don't need a lightbox. A desk lamp is already big next to a miniature, so its shadows are soft enough, and two lamps from the front often do better. If you want one anyway, a matte see-through plastic tub with one side cut away, with lamps shining on its walls from outside, makes a cheap one.

Keep the phone still with a cheap phone tripod or a stack of books, and use the self-timer so tapping the button doesn't shake it. Don't zoom in. Shoot from where it focuses sharply, about 30 cm away, and crop afterwards.

Tap the screen on the model's face to focus, then drag the brightness slider down until the highlights aren't blown out and the contrast looks like the model in your hand. If the phone keeps shifting the colours on its own, a camera app with manual settings lets you fix focus, exposure and white balance.

Afterwards make only small changes to brightness, contrast and white balance, and compare the photo with the real model. Shoot each model the same way every time and your progress photos will line up.

guides.title: Storing terrain and scenery
guides.summary: Plan terrain so it packs flat into a few labelled boxes, and keep it cool, dry, dust free and out of the sun.
body: Think about storage before you glue or paint. Many plastic buildings clip together firmly, so leave walls unglued where the joins are hidden and leave roofs and upper floors loose. They come apart flat, fit in one deep box and leave room for more later.
Test pack the box before painting. Measure the height left once a tray for small scatter pieces is in, and plan the big pieces to fit that space.

Cut foam hills from slabs that span the box, drawn out like a jigsaw so they nest together in layers. Small hills can sit on bigger ones. Extruded foam is tougher and cuts cleaner than bead foam, which crumbles.

Write labels on the underside of each piece, as labels on top get painted over. Number the layers and mark both sides of every join, so repacking after a game takes moments rather than a puzzle session.
Keep scenery somewhere cool and dry, away from sunny windows and out of the car: sun fades paint and can warp resin, and heat softens plastic. Closed boxes or a cupboard keep the dust off.
Scenery gets knocked about in every game, so varnish the pieces that are handled most. Delicate scatter is safer in a foam tray or on a steel sheet with magnets under it.
A board made of foam panels taped edge to edge, with the hinges folding opposite ways, folds flat like a zig-zag and stands against a wall.

guides.title: Making and basing movement trays
guides.summary: A thin steel plate with low side rails moves a whole block of rank-and-file models, based and painted to match their ground.
body: A movement tray carries a whole block of rank-and-file models so the unit moves in one go and nothing gets knocked over. Ready-made ones exist, but they're quick to make.

Work out the block's footprint first: models wide by ranks deep, times the base size. Ten models on 20 mm bases, three ranks deep, is 200 by 60 mm. Add a little space so models aren't jammed in, as some can't sit base to base, and allow for the rails.

Thin steel sheet, under 1 mm, cuts with old scissors. Mark it in pencil, cut it out and file the corners. Steel also holds models with magnets under their bases, so they stay put when the tray is moved.
Cut balsa strips in pairs and super glue them along the edges, flush with the plate. Four sides stop models sliding off in transport; three leave the back open so models can come off easily.
Base the rails like the unit's bases so the tray looks like part of the ground. Brush wood glue on the outer faces only and sprinkle sand on, one side at a time.

Keep glue and sand off the floor of the tray, as a stray grain stops models sitting flat. Brush off anything that lands inside straight away and scrape loose grains out with a knife tip before the glue cures.

Spray the tray black, drybrush the rails up from dark brown to bone, add a few dots of glue with grass, and paint any rim in the same colour as the unit's base rims so the tray disappears under the models.

guides.title: Putting lights in models
guides.summary: Plan small LED lights before you build, run their wires through hollow parts to a battery hidden in the base, and paint the glow round them.
body: Small LED lights can make lenses, screens, holograms, torches or a forge really shine. They take planning, so decide where each light and its wires will go before you glue the model together.

Most plastic figures are hollow inside the torso, so wires can run through it. Drill a hole just wide enough for the wires through the parts in between, such as along an arm to where the light sits, and feed the wires through before you glue.
The battery and any switch need a home: a larger, deeper base, around 32 mm or more for a single figure, or a hollow piece of scenery such as a barrel, crate or building that can hide the wiring.
Many hobby LEDs come with their wires ready to join. If yours don't, strip the ends and twist the matching wires together, and follow the kit's own instructions for which wire goes where.

Fix each tiny LED in its hole with a drop of super glue and a touch of accelerator. Where a wire won't fit, a line of conductive paint can carry the current instead. Slide a short heat shrink sleeve over each join and shrink it as its pack says, so bare wires can't touch, and hold loose wires in place with tack while you fit them.
Flickering LEDs suit torches, fires and forges, or faulty machines and warning lights. Pick the light colour to match the glow you plan to paint.

Before priming, wrap the LED in a little foil held on with tack so it stays clean. Afterwards, paint the glow onto the nearby surfaces as you would for a painted light, so the real light and the painted one agree.

guides.title: The easiest first base
guides.summary: Sand on white glue, a thin brown stain, a pale drybrush and a neat rim make a quick, good looking first base.
body: Start simple. A base hides the plastic disc, ties a group together and makes a model look finished, and sand on glue does all of that with hardly any skill.

Brush white glue over the top of the base with an old brush and wipe the rim clean with a finger. Dip it in sand, or sprinkle fine gravel or dried garden dirt over it, and tap off the extra. Push in a small rock or two if you like.
Let it dry on its own, as a hair dryer can blow the grit off. Dribble thinned glue over any loose patches, or prime the model with the base on so the primer locks the sand down.
Flood very thin brown over the sand so it soaks in, let it dry, then drybrush pale bone or sand lightly over the top. Pick ground lighter than a dark model, or darker than a pale one.
Paint the rim neatly in black or dark brown, angling the brush so the line stops at the top edge. Once the rim is dry, add a tuft or two with tweezers.

Even quicker, a gritty texture paint spread on with an old brush gives grit and colour in one go; then wash, drybrush and paint the rim the same way. Basing tips has full steps for both as Sand and rocks, and Texture paint ground.
