guides.title: Resin print problems: sticky, bulging or brittle
guides.summary: Most sticky, bulging or snapping resin prints come down to washing, curing, trapped resin or the resin itself.
body: A print that still feels sticky or tacky after curing has uncured resin on its surface, and paint won't hold on it for long. Wash it again in strong isopropyl alcohol, or in water if the resin is a water-washable type. Swish or brush it so the liquid reaches every recess, then let it dry fully. Water left on it when it goes under the light dries as a white film.

Then give it more light. Strong midday sun takes roughly an hour, though weak winter sun may barely cure it; a curing lamp or station, even a nail lamp, takes a few minutes, depending on the size of the print. Turn it so every side gets light, the underside of the base included. Air slows curing at the surface, so some painters cure prints sunk in a clear tub of water for a more even result.

A hollow print needs a drain hole. Without one, liquid resin stays trapped inside and never cures, and the air sealed in can expand under the curing light and push out a bulge. Hollowing in the slicer saves resin, but always add a drain hole so the liquid resin inside can run out.

Prints that snap at ankles, spear tips and antennae are partly down to the resin. Standard resins are on the brittle side, and some blends add softer ingredients so the plastic flexes a little before it breaks. Shake the bottle well before every print, as the ingredients settle and an unmixed bottle prints less reliably. Handle thin parts gently.

Faint rings or contour lines on smooth curves come from the layers. A normal coat of primer and paint usually hides light ones. White resin glares and hides flaws, so a thin wash of brown or a solid colour primer first shows up nubs, pits and lines while you can still sand them.

Glue printed resin with super glue; a slightly flexible type is less likely to snap at the joint. Pin heavy or long parts. A snapped spear or antenna is better replaced with metal rod, as in Replacing snapped spears, ankles and thin parts.

Received a print rather than printed it? It should arrive washed and cured. If it feels tacky, wear gloves, then wash and cure it as above if you have the kit, or ask the maker for a replacement rather than painting over it.

Wear nitrile gloves until a print is cured, and keep alcohol well away from heat, as it and its fumes catch fire easily. Never pour resin or used alcohol down the drain. Leave resin-soaked paper towels in the sun to harden before they go in the bin.

guides.title: Failed resin prints and support trouble
guides.summary: When a print sticks to the vat film, loses its toes or comes out pitted, check supports, angle and exposure in turn.
body: Part of the model left stuck to the vat film, or a loose blob in the resin, means that part wasn't held up. Usually an island, a part that starts printing before it joins the rest, had no support, or there were too few supports for the weight above them. Supports carry soft, part cured resin while it prints.

Clear the vat before trying again. Cured flakes from a failed print float in the resin and ruin the next one. Cure a thin skin across the film, using the tank cleaning mode or one blank layer, and peel it out with the bits stuck to it, using a plastic tool, never metal. Looking after a resin printer covers this.

Toes, fingertips and other small tips that print short were not supported. A tip that starts printing in mid air has nothing to build on, so add a support under each one. Automatic supports can miss them, so check every finger and toe yourself. A short tip can be rebuilt with putty, but it's easier to get the supports right.

Pitting or rough marks across the back usually come from automatic supports on a model tipped back steeply. Tilting it back only about 10 degrees and adding supports by hand, stepping through the layers to catch every island, usually keeps that side clean. Put supports where the marks are easy to clean or won't show.

Support marks with a rough texture can be reduced with fewer struts and smaller contact points where the slicer allows. Run supports from the build plate rather than from one part of the model to another, so they come off cleanly.

Soft, blurry detail or prints that fail for no clear reason can be exposure. Every resin cures at its own speed, so run a small test print whenever you change resin and note the settings that work. Room temperature and a slack or scratched film affect prints too, so check those before blaming the settings.
Long prints carry more risk, so check the first layers when you can. Many printers let you pause to top up resin, and a print set at the wrong angle is better restarted early than left to fail.

Take supports off before the final cure. Clip them close to the model with flush cutters rather than pulling, so they don't tear out detail, then trim and sand the nubs as in Preparing 3D printed models.
keywords: half my print stayed on the film

guides.title: Fixing building mistakes on a kit
guides.summary: A part glued on wrong, snapped or lost is rarely the end of a model; most building slips can be undone or hidden.
body: Glued a part on wrong with plastic glue? Act straight away. For a short while the joint is soft and the part can be pulled off or twisted into place. Scrape off the softened plastic before refitting it.

Once plastic glue has set, the parts are welded together. Cut along the seam with a fine razor saw or a sharp blade rather than pulling, file the faces flat and glue again. Expect to fill a small gap afterwards.

Superglue joints are brittle and can usually be snapped apart with a firm twist; a few hours in the freezer first helps. Acetone, such as nail varnish remover, softens superglue, but it can also soften plastic and lift paint, so use very little.

A clean snap, such as a thin sword breaking at its weak point, usually lines up well. Glue it with a tiny drop of superglue, hold it straight until it sets, then smooth the join with a fine emery board. Pin anything that carries weight.
Clipped off a small locating peg? Glue it back with a dab of superglue. It only has to keep the part lined up. Look closely before you clip: some nubs are pegs, not leftover frame.

Lost a part? Search on a hard floor rather than carpet, and next time build over a cloth so parts don't bounce away. A spare from another kit or a small piece of putty sculpting usually covers it, and makers often replace parts missing from a new kit.
Once the glue is fully set, gaps left by a crooked fix can be filled; see Filling gaps between parts.

guides.title: Hollow backs and push-pin marks
guides.summary: Fill shallow round marks with brush-on filler, shave raised ones flat, and pack big hollows with foil before putty.
body: Some figures have hollow backs under cloaks, open undersides on vehicles, or small round marks where the part was pushed out of its mould. Most only show from behind or below, so first decide whether anyone will see them.

Shallow round dips fill like any small gap. Brush a water-based filler in, then draw a damp brush gently outwards so it feathers to nothing. It shrinks as it dries, so expect two or three thin coats, and sand it dry once hard.
Raised round discs can be shaved flat with a sharp blade held almost flat to the surface, then smoothed with a fine sanding stick.

Deeper holes and hollow cloaks take two-part epoxy putty. A soft putty spreads thinly, grips well, shrinks little and sands well once cured, which takes roughly 5 to 6 hours at room temperature. Press it in, smooth it with a wet tool or rubber shaper and leave it overnight before sanding.

For a big hollow, pack crumpled kitchen foil into the space first, then skin it with a thin layer of putty. It saves putty. Sculpt folds into the surface while it's soft, or smooth it flat where it won't show.

On plastic kits, dissolved sprue filler also closes larger gaps and welds into the plastic, though it smells strongly and needs fresh air. On a vehicle's open underside, gluing a piece of plastic card or a spare part over the opening is quicker than filling it.
Check under a strong light after priming. Primer shows any dip you missed, and a second fill and a dab of primer on that spot fixes it.
keywords: hole in the back of a model

guides.title: Spray can spitting, clogged or running low
guides.summary: Blobs, spatter and a weak spray usually come from a cold, badly shaken, clogged or nearly empty can.
body: A can that spits blobs or drizzles instead of giving a fine mist is most often too cold. Keep cans indoors at room temperature. Warm a cold one in lukewarm water for a few minutes, never with direct heat, as an aerosol can burst.
Shake it for longer than feels needed, two minutes or more, and give it a few more shakes between passes. Paint that isn't fully mixed spits and sprays unevenly.
To stop the nozzle clogging, turn the can upside down after each session and spray until only clear gas comes out. That empties the nozzle so paint doesn't dry inside it.

A nearly empty can loses pressure and leaves a speckled, grainy finish that looks blotchy under paint, even when it feels smooth. Start a big batch with a fresh can, and test any can on card or a spare part before it goes near a model.

Blobs also come from spraying too close or holding the button down too long in one spot. Start spraying beside the model, sweep across and release past it, using short bursts from roughly 20 to 30 cm away.

If blobs land on the model, leave them to dry rather than touching them, as wet primer smears. Small ones can be shaved or sanded flat once hard. A heavily spotted or grainy coat is better stripped and done again.
If a can won't behave on a cold day, prime by brush instead. Another way is to undercoat it dark by brush, then overbrush the main colour with a large old brush.

guides.title: Fixing paint chipped off in a game
guides.summary: Touch up a chip with the original colours in small dabs, break up its edge, reseal the patch, then stop it happening again.
body: Chips after a game mostly come from fingers and from models knocking together in a box, so they turn up on raised edges, weapon tips, the base rim and anything that sticks out. Most are a quick fix if you still have the colours.

Brush off dust and loose flakes and check nothing is loose. Reglue or pin a broken part first. On plastic, a coat or two of paint covers a small bare spot without priming; on bare metal, dab on primer first.

Find out what you used. Your saved recipe, a note or a photo of the pots gives the colours and their order. If you have nothing written down, take the nearest match and test it under your lamp on the underside of the base, dry, before it goes near the model.

Rebuild the area in the same order as the first time, just smaller: the base colour in thin coats, a touch of wash if the area was washed, then the highlight. Plain base colour over a washed area leaves a bright patch, so mix in a little of the wash or a darker tone to match.

Don't trace round the chip. A hard, clean edge is what makes a repair show, so dab small uneven patches that cross the old edge on both sides. On a drybrushed or stippled area, a little texture over the patch helps it blend in.

A brushed touch-up over a sprayed colour can dry with a different sheen. Once it's dry, brush a little of the same varnish as the rest over the patch, spreading it a touch past the edges, so the shine matches.
On a battered or weathered model, an awkward chip can simply stay as battle damage. Paint a darker chip colour into it with a fine light line along its lower edge, and it reads as wear.

To stop it happening again, varnish gaming models, with a gloss coat under the matte for extra toughness. Glue magnets under the bases and carry the models on a steel sheet so they can't rub, line case walls with soft fabric, and pick models up by the base.

guides.title: One-coat paints dried blotchy or patchy
guides.summary: Blotches, rings and streaks in one-coat paints come from smooth panels, overloading and brushing back in, and most can be rescued.
body: These paints flow like a wash and dry from the edges inwards, so on big smooth panels, cloaks and rounded legs they gather unevenly and dry with dark patches and rings. Fur, scales and mail hide it. Rough clipper marks and a dusty spray finish give them more places to pool, so smooth upward faces first.

Load from a palette, not the pot, and with less than you think. Blot stray water off the brush first, as it thins the paint unevenly. Put a little extra in one spot, use it as a reservoir to spread across the panel, and run just past the panel edge so you stop at a natural break, not in the middle.

Then leave it. It levels out as it dries, and scrubbing or going back into a half-dry patch tears its skin and leaves streaks a second coat won't hide. Keep the model at the same angle until it's dry so the paint runs one way only. On a blade, draw one stroke down each flat face and let it dry.

Mop pools straight away by touching a clean, damp brush to them. A medium brush soaks up far more than a tiny one. Check low corners and the undersides of overhangs. If the paint has started to dry before you finish, stop and let it dry fully rather than chasing it.

If a colour always streaks, thin it with its clear medium, roughly two parts paint to one of medium, or half and half, and give two thin coats instead of one heavy one. A drop of water is fine, but heavier thinning with water breaks the colour up on smooth surfaces. In hot weather a little more medium gives you longer to work.

On large flat areas, base coat a normal paint of a similar colour first. The one-coat paint goes on far more evenly over it. Or keep one-coat paints for the textured and detailed parts and paint the big smooth panels with opaque paint and painted highlights.

Once fully dry, a second coat put on the same way, panel by panel and in the reverse order to the first, evens out mild patches. A light drybrush of a brighter version of the colour hides blotches and highlights the edges in one go. A thin coat of matte or satin varnish at the end evens out a patchy sheen.

If a smooth panel is badly blotchy, cover it in a few thin coats of a matching opaque colour and highlight it as normal, or paint it back in the primer colour and redo that panel. A blotchy dark panel can take several thin coats of plain black, an edge highlight and a few small scratches.

guides.title: Paint peeling, flaking or rubbing off
guides.summary: Paint that lifts, flakes or rubs off usually comes from grease, missing primer, rushing or handling, so fix the cause, then patch it.
body: Notice when it comes off. Paint that beads or flakes in sheets points to grease or bare plastic under it. Paint that lifts as you brush the next coat wasn't dry. Wear on edges after games is handling. Paint that comes away with tape had not gripped what was under it.

New models carry release agent from the mould, and fingers add skin oil. Paint and primer bead up or flake off both. Scrub parts in warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid and an old toothbrush, rinse, and let them dry fully before priming. Resin and board-game figures often carry the most.

Prime everything. Paint on bare plastic or metal grips poorly, and fresh paint on bare plastic rubs off very easily even once it looks dry, though it toughens over a few days. Let primer dry fully before painting, as painting too soon can pull the primer off with it. Metal chips far more easily than plastic, so varnish metal figures.

Fresh paint is soft. Let each coat dry before the next, as brushing over a half-dry layer drags it up, and thick single coats can crack and peel as they dry. Some washes skin over and peel if touched half dry, so work them while fully wet and then leave them alone. If glazes start lifting the layers below, thin them with plain water rather than flow improver.

Hold the model on a painting handle or by its base so fingers never rub the paint. One-coat paints used straight from the pot and metallic edges rub off fastest. If you have to hold a finished area while you work, brush a coat of varnish over it first. Varnish gaming models once finished, base included.

For masking, use low-tack hobby tape, not household tape, and only on paint that has cured over sound primer. Test a hidden spot first. A thin coat of varnish under the tape helps it peel cleanly. Peel slowly, folding the tape back at a low angle.

To repair a small patch, let it dry, smooth any lifted edge with a fine sanding stick or a light knife scrape, dab brush-on primer onto bare spots, then rebuild the colours in thin coats; Fixing paint chipped off in a game covers matching the colours and hiding the edge. If paint flakes all over, strip it, wash the model well and start again.

If paint came off under oils or enamels, the brush usually did it: scrubbing, too much spirit or paint that was still fresh. Gloss varnish the rest of the model, switch to a softer brush, and hide the damaged spots later as chips.
keywords: paint comes off when i hold it

guides.title: Dust, hairs and fluff stuck in paint
guides.summary: Lift a hair from wet paint at once, pick or sand it out once dry, and dust the model off before primer, varnish and washes.
body: Most specks come from dusty rinse water, the brush itself, tissue or paper towel, clothes and pets, or a model left out between sessions. Primer and varnish fix anything sitting on the surface in place for good, and a later wash collects round it and makes it stand out more.

Change the rinse water when dust or fluff floats in it, especially before smooth base coats, glazes and stippling. Wipe brushes on a lint-free cloth or an old cotton shirt rather than tissue or toilet roll. Flick a drybrush under a bright light to shake out loose fluff before using it, and keep fuzzy jumpers away from the desk.

Dust the model with a soft drybrush or a puff of air just before priming, varnishing or an all-over wash. Don't varnish in a dusty room. Keep a model that is drying covered, and put the lid on the wet palette during breaks.
If a hair lands in wet paint, lift it out at once with the tip of a clean brush or a toothpick, then smooth the paint while it's still wet.

Once the paint is dry, pick the speck out with the point of a sharp blade or a toothpick, using light pressure, and touch the spot up with the same colour. If it left a ridge, smooth it first with a fine sanding stick, or a scrap of fine sandpaper glued to a toothpick for tight spots.
Fluff caught in primer: let it dry, scrape or sand it off, and dab a little brush-on primer over the spot. Primer that feels fuzzy all over is a different problem, from spraying too far away.

A hair sealed under varnish won't lift out cleanly. Either live with it, or let the varnish cure, gently scrape or sand the speck away, touch up the paint and give just that spot a thin coat of varnish again.

guides.title: Basing problems: grass, tufts, sand and paste
guides.summary: Grass that lies flat or falls off, loose tufts, white glue bloom, shedding sand and cracked paste each have a simple cause and fix.
body: Grass fibres need wet glue and a lift to stand up. Dab glue in small patches, press or sprinkle the fibres on while it's wet, then turn the base over and flick the underside hard, or hold a charged balloon just above it. Work a few patches at a time, as glue spread wide loses its grip before it looks dry.

Let the glue dry fully before handling, then tip the base over and brush off the loose strands. A coat of varnish over the grass afterwards stiffens it and holds it in place, and lets you paint or drybrush it to match the base.

Self-adhesive tufts hold far better with a touch of glue under them, especially on uneven ground. Pull the loose strands off the edge of each tuft first, as they fall off anyway. On models that get handled, gel super glue holds tufts better than white glue, which lets them loosen over time.

Super glue can leave a white frosty bloom on the ground and rim round tufts, and it's hard to paint over. Use a tiny amount from a pin rather than the nozzle, keep it away from the rim, and use white glue for loose scatter. Hide a bloom that has already formed under a tuft or a pinch of scatter.

Sand that rubs off was held by too little glue. Once dry, tap off the loose grains, then lock the rest in before painting: drip thinned white glue or a stronger scenic glue onto it from the brush without touching the surface, or mist it with varnish, and leave it overnight. Dab paint on rather than brushing it, so you don't drag grains loose.

Heavy drybrushing scrubs texture loose. Seal sand, grit and dried texture paste with gloss varnish or thinned glue before you drybrush, and fix any skulls or rocks pressed into paste with a dot of glue.

Texture paste and thick crackle split as they dry, and the thicker the layer, the bigger the cracks. For smooth ground, spread it thinner and in two layers, letting each dry. Let paste and glued sand dry naturally, as a hair dryer can skin the paste or crack the glue layer. Porous paste soaks up washes unevenly, so seal it first.
Wipe sand and paste off the rim with a damp finger before they dry. Paint the rim after the texture but before grass and tufts, so nothing sticks in wet rim paint.

guides.title: Metallic glitter in other colours
guides.summary: Find where the flakes came from, cover specks on dry paint with the colour, and layer back over glitter that dried in a wash.
body: Sparkles in a cloak, in skin or in a wash are metal flakes carried over in rinse water, in a brush, on the palette or from a metal drybrush that strayed. Find which it was before you fix anything, or the glitter comes straight back.

Change the rinse water, or keep a separate pot just for metallics, and rinse and wipe the brush well before going back to other colours. Use a clean part of the palette, or keep one area just for metals.

On dry paint, cover the specks with the original colour in one or two thin coats; flakes paint over like anything else. A few big specks can be rubbed off first with the chewed, damp tip of a toothpick, then touched up.

Glitter that dried into a wash won't wash out. Layer the base colour back over the raised areas, as you would after any wash, and redo the recesses with fresh water and a clean brush if they need it. Flakes left lying in recesses after metalwork can be brushed out with a clean drybrush before the wash goes on.
Paint or drybrush the metal parts before tidying the colours next to them, or leave metals until last, so any stray flakes get covered by the next step.

guides.title: Glue marks, melted detail and fingerprints
guides.summary: Plastic glue softens plastic and holds prints, so let it harden, then scrape and sand, and keep glue and fingers off joins and paint.
body: Plastic glue works by melting the surface. Touch the join while it's soft and it keeps your fingerprint; flood it and nearby detail softens into blurry brush marks. Keep thumbs off the join, put glue only on the contact faces, and on tiny contact points use super glue or a bigger joint.

To fix a print or smear, leave it to harden fully, ideally overnight, as soft plastic only smears more. Then scrape the mark level with the edge of a sharp blade and sand it smooth with a fine sanding stick, or a scrap of fine paper glued to a toothpick for tight spots.
A thin brush of extra thin plastic glue over a scuffed or sanded area melts loose fuzz flat and levels small scratches. Use very little and let it dry fully before priming.

Detail that has melted can't be brought back. Sand it smooth so it looks deliberate, rebuild it with a little putty, or cover it with a spare part. On metal or rough surfaces, a dab of crackle or rust texture hides glue smears and fingerprints.

Super glue flooded onto a join can fog nearby detail white, and its fumes cloud clear parts. Put a tiny amount on one surface only, from a pin, and use a clear-parts glue or white glue on canopies. On solid parts a thin film of residue disappears under primer.
Primer shows up glue blobs and sanding marks you missed. Scrape and sand them, then brush primer over just that spot.
Never use plastic glue on painted parts, as it melts the paint too. Scrape the paint off both contact points and join them with a small drop of super glue.

Prints in paint come from oily hands on matte paint, or from handling paint or varnish too soon. Wiping one with a damp sponge can strip the paint, even a day later, so repaint the spot instead. Use a handle or thin disposable gloves on big models, and leave brush-on varnish 12 to 24 hours before handling.

guides.title: Model looks flat, muddy or boring
guides.summary: Work out whether it lacks contrast, has gone muddy, has no focal point or has a dull finish, then follow the guide for that one.
body: Almost every model looks rough halfway through, so finish the main steps before judging. Then take a close phone photo and also look from arm's length. Spotting mistakes with a phone photo covers this, and a photo shows whether the model reads as one grey mass.

Flat means the lights and darks are too close together. Small models need deeper shadows and brighter highlights than feel natural, and fast army painting often stops short of them. See Pushing contrast further, Where highlights go and Edge highlighting.

Muddy or murky usually means a heavy dark wash over everything at the end, black or brown shading on a bright colour, or a dark undercoat under pale paint. Shade each colour with its own family, layer the base colour back over the raised areas, and start brighter than you want to finish. See Keeping colours bright and saturated and Shading without black.

Boring often means one colour everywhere, or only metal and leather with every material painted the same way. One small, strong accent colour near the face, and different highlights for cloth, metal and skin, give the eye somewhere to land. See Adding an accent colour and Creating a focal point.

If it looked right before varnish and dull after, the matte coat went on too thick or flattened the colours; see Varnish changing your colours. A patchwork of shiny and matte areas also looks dull, and one thin coat of varnish over everything evens it out.
If the highlights look chalky or dusty, often after heavy drybrushing, a thin glaze of the base colour over them brings the colour back. See Fixing chalky highlights.
Change one thing at a time, then look again. When you dislike your paint job covers deciding what to fix before you reach for the paint stripper.
keywords: why does my model look bad
